questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman seroconverted for CMV infection during her second pregnancy after a febrile illness in her toddler. Antenatal ultrasound scans were normal. A healthy male infant was delivered at 39 weeks’ gestation.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation of the baby to identify congenital CMV infection?

options.text: Serum CMV IgG and avidity assay

questions.explanation: Urine CMV DNA PCR Neonatal serology is unhelpful as this will only reflect transplacental maternal antibody transfer. The mother is already known to be CMV IgG positive. Urine (or saliva) CMV DNA PCR are the recommended first-line investigations in screening for congenital CMV infection as they are more sensitive than plasma CMV DNA PCR, and the clinical specimens are easily obtained. A positive urine/saliva result should be confirmed with a second sample from any site, and plasma CMV DNA PCR, if positive, may be used to monitor the response to treatment. Lumbar puncture would not routinely be performed on a well infant as a screening test for CMV infection, although CSF CMV DNA PCR might be performed as part of the assessment of an infant found to have congenital CMV infection.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q22

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with HIV , not on therapy, presents to clinic for her first visit. She has had several months of weight loss and intermittent night sweats. She has thrush. She also noted that she has had several weeks of visual changes with “floaters” and blurring of her vision bilaterally. Dilated funduscopic exam was performed, and she was found to have white, perivascular retinal infiltrates and dot-blot hemorrhages.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of these findings?
questions.explanation: Cytomegalovirus CMV is the most common ocular infection in patients living with HIV . It is most common in patients who have CD4 counts <50/μL, and patients often present with complaints of “floaters” and blurred vision. Examination shows necrotizing, full-thickness retinitis, often with some associated hemorrhage, which creates a “brush fire” or “ketchup and cottage cheese” appearance.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q35

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man underwent deceased donor kidney transplant for end-stage renal disease secondary to diabetes mellitus. He received antithymocyte globulin for induction and tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone for maintenance immunosuppression. Investigations: Recipient CMV IgG negative Donor CMV IgG indeterminate
questions.lead_in: What strategy should be recommended to prevent CMV disease?
questions.explanation: Valganciclovir Since the donor had indeterminate CMV serology, and the recipient was CMV seronegative, clinicians should assume that the donor was CMV seropositive since this is the higherrisk possibility and administer prophylaxis accordingly. The standard for CMV D+/R− patients is to administer valganciclovir for 6 months. Valganciclovir is rapidly metabolized to active ganciclovir in the GI tract and liver and may be taken once daily. Use of oral ganciclovir has very low bioavailability and would have a very high pill burden. Foscarnet and cidofovir are only available IV , and their role is for CMV prophylaxis when first-line treatments are contraindicated, or there is resistance. Aciclovir is not active against CMV .
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q25

questions.model_answer:
a) Definitive diagnosis requires demonstration of HCMV in tissue/BAL from the affected lung (quantitative NAAT of BAL fluid, plus antigen detection/immunohistochemistry or culture showing invasive infection); blood viral load alerts to end-organ disease but does not confirm it.
b) (1) UL97 (viral kinase) mutation – confers GCV resistance by reducing GCV phosphorylation; lower-level UL97 resistance may be partly overcome by high-dose ganciclovir. (2) UL54 (viral DNA polymerase) mutation – confers cross-resistance to ganciclovir, foscarnet, and cidofovir; NOT overcome by high-dose ganciclovir (switch to foscarnet).

cohort_answer.text: Definitive diagnosis: clinical symptoms/signs of pneumonia (new infiltrates, hypoxia, tachypnea, dyspnea) combined with CMV documented in lung tissue by virus isolation, rapid culture, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, or DNA hybridization. Mutations: UL54 DNA polymerase mutation (confers resistance to all standard agents - ganciclovir, foscarnet, cidofovir); UL97 kinase mutation (decreases phosphorylation of GCV; multiple mutations conferring 5-15 fold increased IC50; UL97 arises first, >90%; does not affect foscarnet/cidofovir). UL97 mutants can sometimes be overcome with high dose ganciclovir (only mild disease, specific mutations <5-10 fold increase); otherwise treat with foscarnet/cidofovir. UL54 mutations should use foscarnet

questions.model_answer:
a) Viral culture: (1) Prolonged turnaround – slow-growing, cell-associated virus requiring up to 4 weeks before called negative (not useful in real time). (2) Requires viable virus and tissue-culture facilities; sensitivity depends on specimen quality/viral load.
b) IgG/IgM: (1) IgM can persist for weeks to months, limiting its ability to time acquisition; IgG requires seroconversion/serial samples and avidity to estimate chronicity. (2) Limited value in immunocompromised/allograft recipients (attenuated antibody responses; avidity value uncertain; IVIG alters results).
c) Nucleic acid testing: (1) Lack of assay standardization across laboratories/formats (only partly solved by calibration standards), and no universally accepted viral threshold predicting disease. (2) Highly sensitive so may detect latent/non-replicating DNA in whole blood; localized end-organ disease can be missed if only blood is tested.

cohort_answer.text: Viral culture: prolonged processing time, not clinically useful in real time, poor sensitivity, requires viable CMV, not generally used to monitor treatment response due to time requirements. IgG/IgM: not useful for CMV disease diagnosis in transplant due to attenuated/delayed antibody production, not useful for guiding duration of therapy, IVIG alters results, IgM persists for a long time making acute vs non-acute differentiation difficult. Nucleic acid testing: currently no widely accepted viral threshold for predicting CMV disease, lack of assay standardization; highly sensitive, may detect latent CMV, localized disease may not be picked up.

questions.model_answer: Ganciclovir: guanosine analogue phosphorylated first by the CMV UL97 phosphotransferase, then by cellular enzymes, to ganciclovir triphosphate - a competitive inhibitor of dGTP incorporation that preferentially inhibits viral DNA polymerase and slows/stops chain elongation (not an obligate chain terminator). Ganciclovir resistance (2): (1) UL97 mutations/deletions reducing phosphorylation/activation of the drug (most common; usually retains foscarnet and cidofovir susceptibility); (2) UL54 viral DNA polymerase mutations (often with UL97, frequent cross-resistance to cidofovir, usually susceptible to foscarnet). Foscarnet: pyrophosphate analogue that reversibly blocks the pyrophosphate-binding site of viral DNA polymerase, inhibiting replication without requiring phosphorylation. Acyclovir: nucleoside analogue activated by viral TK then cellular kinases to acyclovir triphosphate, which inhibits/inactivates viral DNA polymerase and causes obligate DNA chain termination. Letermovir: inhibits the CMV terminase complex (UL51/UL56), blocking cleavage of concatemeric DNA into unit genomes for packaging; CMV-only, no effect on DNA polymerase.

cohort_answer.text: Ganciclovir: competes with deoxyguanosine triphosphate to inhibit viral DNA polymerase and block viral DNA synthesis; primarily reserved for CMV, also active against HSV-1/2 (same mechanism as valganciclovir). Resistance: UL97 gene mutation (most common, occurs prior to UL54, causes deficiency in viral kinase for ganciclovir phosphorylation/activation, cidofovir and foscarnet usually retain efficacy) and UL54 mutation (often co-exists with UL97, changes viral DNA polymerase, cross-resistance to cidofovir common, cross-resistance to foscarnet rare; HSV isolates resistant to acyclovir due to absent TK are also resistant to ganciclovir). Foscarnet: inorganic pyrophosphate analog, selectively inhibits viral DNA polymerase by blocking pyrophosphate binding sites, suppressing viral replication; resistance occurs secondary to some but not all UL54 mutations; primarily reserved for ganciclovir-resistant CMV, also effective against HSV/VZV including acyclovir-resistant isolates; main adverse effect is nephrotoxicity (dose-limiting, minimized with hydration). Acyclovir: synthetic purine nucleoside analog with high affinity for HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV thymidine kinase which phosphorylates/activates the drug; human cellular guanylate kinase further phosphorylates it to acyclovir triphosphate, which blocks viral DNA synthesis by competitively inhibiting/inactivating viral DNA polymerase and causing DNA chain termination (valacyclovir, penciclovir, famciclovir have similar mechanisms; cidofovir similar but does not require viral TK). Letermovir: inhibits the CMV terminase complex (novel mechanism), which normally cleaves long DNA chains produced during CMV replication into single functional units; only active against CMV; FDA approved for CMV prophylaxis in adult CMV-seropositive allogeneic HSCT recipients; low barrier to resistance in vitro; no dosage adjustment needed with CrCl >10 mL/min.

questions.model_answer: Ganciclovir: activated by the CMV UL97 kinase then cellular kinases to ganciclovir triphosphate, which competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase and halts DNA chain elongation. Foscarnet: pyrophosphate analogue that directly blocks the pyrophosphate-binding site of viral DNA polymerase (no phosphorylation needed). Letermovir: inhibits the CMV terminase complex (UL51/UL56), blocking cleavage/packaging of viral DNA. Two ganciclovir-resistance mutations: (1) UL97 - phosphotransferase gene; impairs intracellular phosphorylation/activation of ganciclovir (affects the drug-activation step in the cell; foscarnet/cidofovir usually still active); (2) UL54 - viral DNA polymerase gene; alters the enzyme acting at viral DNA synthesis in the nucleus (frequent cidofovir cross-resistance, foscarnet usually retained).

questions.model_answer:
a) The CMV terminase enzyme complex, specifically the UL56 subunit (the complex comprises UL51, UL56, with UL89); UL56 mutation mediates letermovir resistance.
b) The terminase complex cleaves concatemeric viral DNA into unit-length genomes and packages them into capsids; letermovir binds and inhibits this terminase, blocking DNA cleavage/packaging and viral maturation. questions.question: Give three reasons to use the CMV antigenemia or PCR assay.

parts.text: Give three reasons to use the CMV antigenemia or PCR assay.

parts_raw.text: A. Give three reasons to use the CMV antigenemia or PCR assay

questions.model_answer: a) (1) To guide/initiate pre-emptive antiviral therapy through quantitative monitoring of CMV in blood. (2) To monitor response to antiviral treatment. (3) To detect infection after discontinuing prophylaxis and (for NAAT) to detect development of antiviral resistance; NAAT also gives rapid, standardized, quantitative results applicable to blood, body fluids and tissue.

cohort_answer.text:
CMV Antigenemia Assay: rapidly and directly detects CMV proteins (pp65) in peripheral blood WBC - detects labeled monoclonal Ab specific to pp65 lower matrix protein of CMV. High specificity. Can be done in BAL, blood and tissue samples. Results available within 24h. Antigenemia correlates with viremia in HIV infected pts and recipients of SOT. LIMITATIONS: lack of stability of whole blood specimen, lack of standardization, subjective interpretation, need for sufficient neutrophil numbers (can't do in neutropenia), rather less sensitive in neutropenia, sample processing required within 6-8 hours of collection, labor intensive, unable to detect free virus in fluids.
CMV PCR Assay: High sensitivity. Can use for diagnosing active CMV, monitoring response to therapy. Tissue specific PCR is useful. Sterile fluid PCR is useful (eg vitreous fluid). Can use plasma or whole blood specimens - VL higher and DNA more frequently detected in whole blood than in plasma; low levels of CMV DNA do not always correlate with CMV disease. CMV DNA is stable in whole blood and plasma for up to 5d when stored at 4 degrees C. There are still variabilities between different assays used, even though WHO developed a 'standardization' in 2010, therefore hard to have a hard cutoff

questions.model_answer:
a) Viral culture: (1) Slow - HCMV grows slowly and cultures must be held up to 4 weeks (prolonged culture, up to 28 days). (2) Labor-intensive and insensitive, requiring tissue-culture facilities; sensitivity depends on specimen quality and viral load (poor in blood).
b) CMV IgM and IgG: (1) IgM can persist for weeks to months, so it does not reliably time acquisition of infection. (2) IgG requires paired/serial samples to demonstrate seroconversion, limiting its value for timely diagnosis of acute infection.
c) PCR/NAT: (1) Cannot distinguish latent from actively replicating virus (CMV DNA is detectable from latently infected leukocytes). cohort_answer.text: Viral Culture: Grows slowly (1-6 weeks); Lacks sensitivity particularly blood; useful in congenital CMV - urine and tissue. CMV IgM and IgG: Requirement for paired serum samples limits utility of timely diagnosis; IgM may persist for several months so stand-alone may provide misleading information (may represent prior infection rather than current). PCR/NAT: Cannot distinguish between active latent and actively replicating virus; unable to differentiate low-level from high-level replication (need quantitative PCR); despite WHO international standard units, there is still variability in viral load values

a) Ganciclovir: phosphorylated first by the viral UL97 kinase then by cellular kinases to ganciclovir triphosphate, which competitively inhibits the viral DNA polymerase (UL54) with respect to dGTP and slows/stops viral DNA chain elongation (not an obligate chain terminator).
b) Letermovir: inhibits the viral terminase complex (UL56/UL51/UL89), blocking cleavage and packaging of viral DNA; no phosphorylation required and no DNA-polymerase inhibition.
c) Foscarnet: pyrophosphate analogue that directly inhibits the viral DNA polymerase (UL54) at the pyrophosphate-binding site; requires no phosphorylation.
d) Maribavir: inhibits the UL97 protein kinase, reducing phosphorylation of UL44 and other proteins, thereby inhibiting viral DNA synthesis and blocking nuclear egress of virions.

(2) UL54 gene mutation (viral DNA polymerase) - point mutations cause ganciclovir resistance and can confer cross-resistance to cidofovir and foscarnet.

Foscarnet - binds UL54 DNA polymerase pyrophosphate site. Maribavir - pUL97 kinase inhibitor. Resistance mutations: point mutations in viral DNA polymerase (UL54 gene) - may cause resistance to ganciclovir/foscarnet/cidofovir (some knock out all three); reduced intracellular ganciclovir phosphorylation from point mutations/deletions in phosphotransferase encoded by UL97 gene (susceptible to foscarnet/cidofovir).

a) Ganciclovir: a deoxyguanosine nucleoside analogue that requires phosphorylation by the CMV UL97 kinase then host kinases to its triphosphate, which inhibits the viral DNA polymerase (UL54) and acts as a DNA chain terminator. Letermovir: inhibits the function of UL51 and UL56 of the HCMV terminase complex (UL51/UL56/UL89), blocking cleavage/packaging of viral DNA and virion maturation. Foscarnet: a pyrophosphate analogue that directly inhibits the viral DNA polymerase (binds the pyrophosphate-binding site of UL54); does not require phosphorylation. Maribavir: directly inhibits the HCMV UL97 protein kinase, blocking viral morphogenesis and DNA-polymerase function.
b) (1) UL97 gene - mutation/deletion in the viral phosphotransferase (kinase); reduces intracellular phosphorylation of ganciclovir, conferring ganciclovir resistance (virus remains susceptible to foscarnet and cidofovir). (2) UL54 gene - mutation in the viral DNA polymerase (target site of ganciclovir triphosphate, cidofovir and foscarnet); confers resistance to ganciclovir, cidofovir, foscarnet and brincidofovir.

cohort_answer.text:
Ganciclovir - binds UL54 catalytic site of DNA polymerase causing cessation of DNA chain elongation (after phosphorylation by UL97 kinase). Letermovir - binds UL51/56 DNA terminase complex enzyme, inhibits viral maturation by preventing cleavage into functional units. Foscarnet - binds the UL54 DNA pol pyrophosphate site suppressing viral replication. Maribavir - pUL97 kinase inhibitor (antagonizes ganciclovir).
Resistance mutations: Reduced intracellular ganciclovir phosphorylation caused by point mutations or deletions in the phosphotransferase (kinase) encoded by the UL97 gene (resistant to ganciclovir, susceptible to foscarnet and cidofovir). Point mutations in viral DNA polymerase UL54 gene result in resistance to ganciclovir and cidofovir, usually still susceptible to foscarnet.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Seropositive recipient (R+; D+/R+ or D-/R+ is the high-risk group in HSCT). (2) HLA mismatch between donor and recipient. (3) Use of T-lymphocyte-depleting strategies (antithymocyte globulin or alemtuzumab). (4) Umbilical cord stem cell transplant into a seropositive recipient. (5) Graft-versus-host disease requiring steroid therapy (HLA-haploidentical HSCT is a further factor).
b) Prophylaxis: antiviral is given to all at-risk recipients regardless of viral detection, for a defined period after transplant (often to ~day 100), frequently followed by a pre-emptive strategy once prophylaxis stops. Pre-emptive therapy: serial quantitative virologic monitoring (qPCR/antigenemia) is performed and antiviral treatment is started only when a predetermined threshold of replication is reached, continuing until resolution or significant reduction of virus.
c) Ganciclovir is not appreciably metabolized and is excreted almost unchanged into the urine; dosing therefore depends on renal function, so dose adjustment is required in patients with renal impairment.
d) UL97 (impaired phosphorylation): (1) foscarnet, (2) cidofovir, (3) letermovir (maribavir also active). UL54 (altered DNA polymerase, cross-resistant to GCV/foscarnet/cidofovir): letermovir (terminase inhibitor, activity independent of UL54).

Define pre-emptive and prophylaxis strategies (no advantages/disadvantages, just describe)
How is IV ganciclovir metabolized, and when might the dose need adjusting
For resistant CMV disease, name three antivirals that may be considered for UL97 mutation and one for UL54 mutation.

questions.model_answer:
a) Five risk factors for CMV disease after HSCT: (1) Recipient CMV-seropositive status (D+/R+ or D-/R+ = high risk in HSCT). (2) HLA mismatch (related donor with one HLA-A/-B/-DR mismatch, or unrelated donor with one HLA-A/-B/-C/-DR mismatch). (3) Use of T-lymphocyte-depleting strategies (antithymocyte globulin or alemtuzumab). (4) Umbilical-cord-blood HSCT into a seropositive recipient, or HLA-haploidentical HSCT. (5) Graft-versus-host disease requiring steroid therapy.
b) Pre-emptive therapy: serial quantitative virologic monitoring of blood/body fluids for CMV replication, with antiviral therapy initiated only once a predetermined viral threshold is reached, continued until the infection resolves or the viral load falls substantially. Prophylaxis: administration of antiviral drug to all at-risk patients from early post-transplant regardless of viral load, to prevent infection (often followed by a pre-emptive strategy once prophylaxis stops).
c) Ganciclovir is not appreciably metabolized; it is excreted almost unchanged in the urine (intracellularly it is phosphorylated by the CMV UL97 kinase then by host kinases to the active triphosphate, but the drug itself undergoes renal, not hepatic, clearance). Therefore the dose must be adjusted according to renal function (renal impairment/dialysis).
d) UL97 mutation (confers ganciclovir resistance; virus remains susceptible to other-target agents): (1) Foscarnet, (2) Cidofovir, (3) Maribavir (a UL97 kinase inhibitor active against GCV-resistant virus). UL54 (DNA polymerase) mutation, which confers cross-resistance to ganciclovir, cidofovir and foscarnet: Maribavir (acts on UL97, not the polymerase).

cohort_answer.text: Risk factors: CMV seropositivity (D-/R+); T cell depletion (ATG); GVHD; Immunosuppressive drugs (steroids, alemtuzumab); Lymphopenia. Pre-emptive therapy: Patients monitored frequently (weekly) with CMV load and antiviral therapy initiated when viral replication reaches a certain assay threshold defined at each institution. Prophylaxis: Immediate start of prophylaxis (ganciclovir, valganciclovir, letermovir) post-transplant in high risk patients. Ganciclovir metabolism: Acyclic analog of nucleoside guanosine, converted intracellularly to ganciclovir 5'-monophosphate by viral kinase encoded by CMV gene UL97 during infection; cellular kinases catalyze formation of ganciclovir diphosphate and triphosphate (10-fold greater concentration in CMV infected cells); ganciclovir triphosphate is a competitive inhibitor of dGTP incorporation into DNA, preferentially inhibiting viral DNA polymerases, and is a poor substrate for chain elongation, disrupting viral DNA synthesis. Dose adjustment needed: Renal impairment; Dialysis; Pre-emptive therapy (induction 5mg/kg q12 vs maintenance 5mg/kg q24); UL97 mutation for <5x (10mg/kg q12, off-label); Intravitreal injection (off-label). Resistant CMV: UL97 mutation - Foscarnet, Cidofovir, Maribavir, possibly high dose ganciclovir. UL54 mutation - Maribavir, Foscarnet (avoid cidofovir)
